title: Foods in the Qur'an and the Sunnah
author: Original guide — verses, hadiths and current nutrition research
source: Coran, hadiths authentifiés et recherche scientifique actuelle (voir chapitre Sources)

chapters.title: Se soigner et prévenir en islam
chapters.text:
## Why this guide

The Qur'an names specific foods. Not in passing: the date appears some twenty times, the olive tree seven, an entire sura carries the name of the bees, and God swears by the fig and the olive. Some fruits describe Paradise; others are given as a remedy at the heart of a narrative — the date offered to Maryam as she went into labour.

This guide starts from a simple question: what do we know today about these foods? Not to "prove" the Qur'an — it has no need of that, and making faith depend on the scientific results of the moment is a weakness, not a strength. But because it is fascinating to see what contemporary research finds, or fails to find, when it turns to these foods.

Every chapter follows the same logic: first the texts — verses and hadiths quoted in full, with their references — then what the research says, with its findings and its limits. Where the evidence is solid, that is stated. Where it is lacking, that is stated too.

## Seeking treatment: an obligation, not resignation

A common misreading holds that faith means enduring illness. The prophetic tradition says exactly the opposite.

*"Servants of Allah, seek treatment! For Allah has sent down no illness without also sending down its cure — save one: old age."* (Reported by Usama ibn Sharik — Sunan at-Tirmidhi, Abu Dawud)

*"For every illness there is a cure. When the cure reaches the illness, the patient recovers by Allah's permission."* (Sahih Muslim)

These words establish an active stance: seeking the remedy is an act of faith, not a challenge to the divine decree. They carried centuries of Arab-Muslim medicine — from ar-Razi to Ibn Sina, whose *Canon* was taught in European universities into the seventeenth century.

There is a flip side. The Prophet ﷺ warned against practising medicine without competence:

*"Whoever practises medicine without being known as a physician is answerable for it."* (Sunan Abu Dawud, Ibn Majah)

A requirement of competence, set out fourteen centuries before professional licensing bodies.

## Prevention rather than cure

**Avoiding danger.** The Qur'an lays down a direct principle: *"And do not throw yourselves into destruction with your own hands."* (Qur'an 2:195). On epidemics, the prophetic instruction is strikingly modern:

*"If you hear of a plague in a land, do not enter it. And if it breaks out in a land where you are, do not leave it in flight."* (Sahih al-Bukhari)

The very principle of quarantine, stated before any germ theory.

**Not making life hard for oneself.** *"Allah intends ease for you, He does not intend hardship for you."* (Qur'an 2:185) — this is the foundation of the dispensations granted to the sick and the traveller: dry ablution, shortened prayer, exemption from fasting.

**Eating without excess.** Two markers frame the diet. The first is Qur'anic:

*"Eat and drink, but do not commit excess. He does not love those who go beyond bounds."* (Qur'an 7:31)

The second is prophetic, and striking in its precision:

*"The son of Adam fills no vessel worse than his stomach. A few mouthfuls suffice to keep him upright. If he must have more, then a third for his food, a third for his drink, a third for his breath."* (Reported by al-Miqdam ibn Ma'dikarib — Sunan at-Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah)

The rule of thirds sums up on its own much of what modern nutrition calls portion control.

**Stilling the heart.** Prevention is not only physical. *"Is it not by the remembrance of Allah that hearts find rest?"* (Qur'an 13:28). The impact of chronic stress on cardiovascular, immune and metabolic health is now extensively documented — this dimension is anything but incidental.

## What this guide is not

This is not a book of prescriptions. The foods presented here are foods: they nourish, they supply useful compounds, and they belong within an overall diet. For any health question, ask your doctor.

chapters.title: La datte
chapters.cat: Les aliments cités dans le Coran
chapters.text:
## In the Qur'an

The palm (*nakhl*) and the palm grove are mentioned some twenty times in the Qur'an, almost always tied to divine bounty and to fertile gardens:

- *"And out of the palm tree's emerging spathe come clusters of dates hanging low"* (Qur'an 6:99)
- *"It is He who produced gardens trellised and untrellised, and palm trees, and crops of diverse taste"* (Qur'an 6:141)
- *"In both are fruit and palm trees and pomegranates"* (Qur'an 55:68)
- *"And We caused to grow within it grain, and grapes and herbage, and olive and palm trees"* (Qur'an 80:27-29)
- *"And from the fruits of the palm trees and grapevines you take intoxicant and good provision"* (Qur'an 16:67)

The most striking passage remains Maryam's. Seized by the pains of childbirth, alone, she receives this command:

*"Shake toward you the trunk of the palm tree; it will drop upon you ripe, fresh dates. So eat and drink and be glad."* (Qur'an 19:25-26)

A fruit named, precisely, for a woman in labour — and we shall see below that this detail has caught researchers' attention.

## In the Sunnah

- *"Whoever takes seven Ajwa dates every morning will not be harmed that day by poison or sorcery."* (Sahih al-Bukhari)
- *"A household that has no dates, its people go hungry."* (Reported by Aisha — Sahih Muslim)
- The Prophet ﷺ broke his fast with fresh dates; failing that, dried dates; failing that, a few sips of water. (Sunan Abu Dawud, at-Tirmidhi)
- He practised *tahnik*: rubbing the palate of newborns with date paste, while supplicating to Allah for them. (Sahih al-Bukhari)
- Asking his companions about "a tree that resembles the Muslim and never sheds its leaves", he himself named the palm. (Sahih al-Bukhari)

## What the research says

**Childbirth: the Qur'anic intuition put to the test.** The link between the date and childbirth has been the subject of several clinical trials and then of meta-analyses, one published in *BMC Pregnancy and Childbirth* (2020). The protocol studied is remarkably close to Maryam's account: about **seven dates a day (≈ 80 g) over the last 2 to 4 weeks of pregnancy**. The findings converge:
- less recourse to induction and augmentation of labour;
- greater cervical dilation on admission to the maternity ward;
- shorter latent phase and second stage of labour;
- in one study, spontaneous labour in 84% of women who ate dates against 61% in the control group.

The authors point to methodological limits in several of the trials included and call for more rigorous work: this is a serious and coherent line of evidence, not yet a validated obstetric protocol.

**A sugar gentler than it looks.** Despite a sugar content of 70 to 76%, the glycaemic index of dates falls between 42 and 75 depending on variety and ripeness — often in the low-to-moderate range, thanks to the fibre that comes with them. A randomised trial published in *Nutrients* (2022) observed that eating dates preserved glycaemic control in patients with type 2 diabetes. Moderation still applies, but the fruit is not the equivalent of an isolated fast sugar.

**Breaking the fast.** The prophetic choice of the date at iftar has a simple physiological explanation: on an empty stomach, its simple sugars accompanied by water are absorbed within minutes, whereas a complex meal takes several hours to restore blood glucose.

**Pits and the Ajwa variety.** A randomised clinical trial tested Ajwa date-pit powder in hyperlipidaemic patients, with effects measured on the lipid profile and blood pressure. Research on Ajwa flesh and pits centres above all on their richness in phenolic compounds and flavonoids.

## Composition (per 100 g)

| Component | Amount |
|---|---|
| Carbohydrates | 63.9 – 76 g |
| Fibre | 8.5 – 10 g |
| Protein | 1.9 – 2.5 g |
| Fat | traces |
| Potassium | 750 mg |
| Calcium | 65 – 68 mg |
| Phosphorus | 64 – 72 mg |
| Magnesium | 59 mg |
| Iron | 1.6 – 5.1 mg |
| Sodium | 5 mg |

About 250 to 300 kcal per 100 g (10 to 12 dates). The potassium-to-sodium ratio — 750 mg against 5 mg — is particularly favourable for blood pressure.

## Varieties

Three categories: **dry** (Deglet Nour, Degla, Zahidi), **semi-dry** (Amry, Ajlany) and **fresh** (Sukkari, Barhi). Among the best known: the Algerian **Deglet Nour**, the Moroccan **Medjool**, the **Ajwa** of Madinah — the very one named in the hadith of the seven morning dates.

## The point to keep

The fruit most often named in the Qur'an is also the one whose precise use — childbirth, indicated to Maryam — has been most directly taken up and tested by contemporary clinical research.

chapters.title: Le raisin
chapters.cat: Les aliments cités dans le Coran
chapters.text:
## In the Qur'an

The vine (*a'nab*) almost always accompanies the palm in the Qur'an's descriptions of fertile gardens:

- *"And out of the palm tree's spathe We bring forth gardens of grapevines"* (Qur'an 6:99)
- *"And within the earth are neighbouring plots and gardens of grapevines…"* (Qur'an 13:4)
- *"He causes to grow for you thereby the crops, olives, palm trees, grapevines"* (Qur'an 16:11)
- *"And We brought forth for you thereby gardens of palm trees and grapevines"* (Qur'an 23:19)
- *"Indeed, for the righteous is attainment: gardens and grapevines"* (Qur'an 78:31-32)

One verse deserves particular attention:

*"And from the fruits of the palm trees and grapevines you take intoxicant and good provision."* (Qur'an 16:67)

Revealed before the definitive prohibition of wine, it already distinguishes two uses of the same fruit: one that leads astray, one that nourishes. The grape, in the Qur'an, stands on the side of "good provision".

## In the Sunnah

Ibn Qayyim al-Jawziyya reports that the Prophet ﷺ was fond of grapes and melons. A hadith attributed to Ibn Abbas describes him eating grapes in quantity, but its chain of transmission is contested by several hadith scholars — caution is therefore warranted on this particular point.

## What the research says

**Resveratrol.** This polyphenol, concentrated in the skin of the grape — especially the black grape — is one of the most studied plant compounds in the world. Two randomised placebo-controlled trials showed that a year's supplementation with a grape extract supplying 8 mg/day of resveratrol improved inflammatory and atherogenic status in subjects at cardiovascular risk as well as in confirmed coronary patients.

**An essential caveat about doses.** The spectacular effects often attributed to resveratrol come from studies using concentrated extracts, at doses no realistic dietary intake reaches. Eating grapes supplies resveratrol, but in far smaller quantity. Both the Linus Pauling Institute and the Cleveland Clinic stress that the evidence in humans remains distinctly more modest than the media enthusiasm.

**The whole fruit beats the molecule.** Research is now moving toward the view that the benefit of the grape lies in the synergy of its components — polyphenols, anthocyanins, fibre, potassium — rather than in an isolated molecule. Effects reported for whole grapes include anti-inflammatory, cardioprotective, vasorelaxant and neuroprotective properties.

**Composition.** About 15% carbohydrate (of which 7% glucose), 0.8% protein, 0.5% fat, roughly 68 kcal per 100 g. The skin concentrates the B-group vitamins and the polyphenols; the flesh supplies vitamin C, potassium, calcium, phosphorus and iron.

## Grape cures: what you should know

The grape has a long history of "cures" — periods in which it becomes the main food, sometimes the only one. These practices, popularised in the twentieth century by figures in naturopathy, have at times been presented as a cancer treatment.

Let us be clear: **none of these claims has ever been validated by clinical research**. A prolonged single-food diet exposes you to serious protein and fat deficiencies, and delaying an established oncological treatment endangers life. What remains defensible is far more modest: a few days of a diet rich in fresh fruit, in a healthy person, replacing no treatment whatever.

**A practical precaution.** Non-organic grapes receive pesticide treatments; wash them thoroughly before eating.

## The point to keep

A fruit the Qur'an explicitly places on the side of "good provision", rich in polyphenols that have genuinely been studied — provided you eat it as a fruit, and do not turn it into a miracle cure.

chapters.title: La figue
chapters.cat: Les aliments cités dans le Coran
chapters.text:
## In the Qur'an

The fig gives its name to an entire sura, *At-Tin*, which opens with a solemn oath:

*"By the fig and the olive! And by Mount Sinai! And by this secure city! We have certainly created man in the best of stature."* (Qur'an 95:1-4)

This is the only mention of the fig tree in the whole Qur'an — but it carries considerable weight. The oath brings together four markers: two nourishing trees, the mountain of the revelation to Moses, and Makkah. Classical commentators read a progression in it: from the food of the body to that of the soul, up to the reminder of the human being's original dignity.

## What the research says

**A fruit exceptionally rich in calcium.** This is the fig's singularity: about **133 mg of calcium per 100 g** of dried figs, more than 10% of the recommended daily intake — a rare level for a fruit, and of real interest for diets low in dairy. The potassium it contains also helps limit the urinary calcium losses linked to an over-salted diet.

**Constipation: clinical trials.** The fig is one of the few fruits whose laxative effect has been tested in a controlled trial. A randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial conducted in South Korea evaluated a fig paste in adults with chronic constipation — with a placebo identical in taste, smell and appearance. A randomised clinical trial has also shown significant improvement in the symptoms of constipation-predominant irritable bowel syndrome: frequency of pain, bloating, stool frequency and stool hardness. Another trial tested a fig-and-walnut syrup in constipated pregnant women.

**Composition.** Rich in fibre, notably soluble fibre (pectins), useful both for transit and for cholesterol regulation. It supplies vitamins A, B1, B2, B6, C and K, along with potassium, magnesium, phosphorus and iron. Its bioactive compounds — phenolic acids, flavonoids, carotenoids, anthocyanins — are the subject of research into antibacterial, hepatoprotective and glucose-regulating properties.

**Fresh or dried: not the same thing.** Drying concentrates everything: the dried fig contains four to five times more sugar than the fresh one. An excellent source of fibre and calcium, it calls for a measured quantity where blood glucose is being watched.

## The point to keep

A fruit by which God swears an oath, and which turns out to be one of the few serious plant sources of calcium — with an effect on intestinal transit genuinely tested in a controlled clinical trial.

chapters.title: L'olive et l'huile d'olive
chapters.cat: Les aliments cités dans le Coran
chapters.text:
## In the Qur'an

The olive tree is one of the plants most present in the Qur'an — some seven mentions — and the only one, together with the fig, to open a sura with a divine oath:

*"By the fig and the olive! And by Mount Sinai! And by this secure city! We have certainly created man in the best of stature."* (Qur'an 95:1-4)

It also appears at the heart of the Verse of Light, one of the most commented upon in the Qur'an:

*"Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth. The example of His light is like a niche within which is a lamp. The lamp is within glass, the glass as if it were a brilliant star, lit from a blessed tree, an olive, neither of the east nor of the west, whose oil would almost glow even if untouched by fire."* (Qur'an 24:35)

And among the nourishing crops:

*"He causes to grow for you thereby the crops, olives, palm trees, grapevines, and of all the fruits."* (Qur'an 16:11)

## In the Sunnah

*"Eat olive oil and anoint yourselves with it, for it comes from a blessed tree."* (Reported by at-Tirmidhi)

*"Take olive oil and rub yourselves with it, for it is a blessed tree."* (Reported by ad-Darimi)

Two uses are therefore explicitly recommended: ingestion, and application to the body.

## What the research says

**The PREDIMED trial.** This is one of the most important nutrition trials ever conducted: 7,447 Spanish adults at high cardiovascular risk, randomised between a Mediterranean diet enriched with extra-virgin olive oil, a Mediterranean diet enriched with nuts, or a low-fat diet. Published in the *New England Journal of Medicine*, it showed after a median follow-up of 4.8 years a **reduction of about 30% in major cardiovascular events** (heart attack, stroke, cardiovascular death) in the extra-virgin olive oil arm.

A point of scientific honesty: the original 2013 publication was retracted in 2018 after irregularities were found in the randomisation procedure at some centres. The data were reanalysed and republished in the *NEJM* the same year — the main conclusions held. Reporting this history does not weaken the result: on the contrary, it shows how science corrects itself.

**Extra-virgin, not just any oil.** A later analysis of the PREDIMED data is illuminating: **extra-virgin** olive oil is associated with a substantial reduction in cardiovascular risk, whereas ordinary refined olive oil, stripped of polyphenols, shows distinctly weaker associations. So it is not only the fat that counts, but what refining destroys.

**The compounds involved.** Oleic acid (a monounsaturated fatty acid) makes up most of the fat. The polyphenols — oleocanthal, hydroxytyrosol — are concentrated in extra-virgin, first cold-pressed oils; oleocanthal in particular is studied for an anti-inflammatory activity comparable in mechanism to that of ibuprofen, at an obviously far smaller dose.

**Use on the skin.** The application recommended by the hadith remains a widespread traditional cosmetic use. Studies on topical olive oil are fewer than those on its dietary use; some suggest usefulness as an emollient, others note that it can disrupt the skin barrier on atopic infant skin — so it is better to stay measured on this particular use.

## The point to keep

Of all the foods named in the Qur'an, extra-virgin olive oil is the one with the highest level of evidence in cardiovascular prevention — from a large randomised trial, not from mere observation.

chapters.title: La grenade
chapters.cat: Les aliments cités dans le Coran
chapters.text:
## In the Qur'an

The pomegranate is named three times, always in a register of abundance — that of the gardens of the earth as of Paradise:

*"In both are fruit and palm trees and pomegranates."* (Qur'an 55:68)

*"And gardens of grapevines and olives and pomegranates."* (Qur'an 6:99)

*"And it is He who produced gardens, trellised and untrellised, and palm trees and crops of different yield, and olives and pomegranates, similar and dissimilar. Eat of their fruit when they yield, and give its due on the day of its harvest. And be not excessive, for He does not love those who commit excess."* (Qur'an 6:141)

This last verse is remarkable: it does not merely name the fruit, it attaches two principles to it — the poor's right over the harvest, and the prohibition of waste.

## What the research says

The pomegranate is one of the most studied fruits of the last two decades, with an unusual volume of human clinical trials.

**Blood pressure.** A recent randomised controlled trial in adults aged 55 to 70 observed a significant fall in systolic blood pressure in the group receiving a pomegranate extract. Another randomised trial reported, at 28 days, significant reductions in systolic and diastolic pressure, in pulse wave velocity (a marker of arterial stiffness) and in fat mass, with an increase in lean mass.

**LDL oxidation and atherosclerosis.** Pomegranate polyphenols reduce the capacity of macrophages to oxidise LDL — a key step in plaque formation — by neutralising reactive oxygen and nitrogen species. They also raise serum paraoxonase activity, an enzyme that hydrolyses the lipid peroxides present in oxidised lipoproteins and atherosclerotic lesions. In cardiac patients, a reduction in carotid intima-media thickness has been reported.

**Platelet function.** Pomegranate polyphenols inhibit platelet aggregation — a mechanism that would explain part of the cardiovascular benefit seen in high-risk patients.

**The active compounds.** Punicalagins are hydrolysable tannins present in exceptional concentration in this fruit — above all in the rind and the white membranes, which are usually thrown away. The seeds contain punicic acid, a fatty acid studied for anti-inflammatory properties. The arils supply vitamins C and K and fibre.

**Two precautions.**
- Concentrated pomegranate juice is calorific and sweet: the benefits measured in the studies do not justify unlimited consumption.
- Like grapefruit, pomegranate can interfere with the hepatic metabolism of certain medicines. If you are on long-term treatment — anticoagulants or statins in particular — it is best to discuss it with your doctor.

## The point to keep

The fruit the Qur'an ties to sharing and to the refusal of waste turns out to be, alongside olive oil, one of the best documented in cardiovascular health — with measured effects on blood pressure and on cholesterol oxidation.

chapters.title: La banane
chapters.cat: Les aliments cités dans le Coran
chapters.text:
## In the Qur'an

The banana appears in the description of the Paradise promised to the "companions of the right":

*"The companions of the right — what are the companions of the right? [They will be] among lote trees with thorns removed, and banana trees layered with fruit, and shade extended, and water poured out, and fruit in abundance, neither limited nor forbidden."* (Qur'an 56:27-33)

The term used is *talh mandud* — literally "*talh* with clusters piled one upon another". Most classical commentators, Ibn Abbas among them, understood it as the banana tree; others read it as a tree of dense shade. The fruit is described there by a double negative that says everything about Paradise: *neither limited, nor forbidden*.

## The banana plant

It is not a tree but a giant herbaceous plant of the Musaceae family: its "trunk" is a stack of leaf sheaths. Each plant fruits only once, then dies leaving a sucker — a striking image of the succession of generations. One bunch carries ten to twenty hands of bananas.

In ancient India the fruit was nicknamed "the philosophers' meal": Hindu sages sheltered under its broad leaves to meditate and fed on it. Pliny the Elder mentions it in his natural history.

## What the research says

**Potassium and blood pressure.** With about 350 to 400 mg of potassium per 100 g, the banana is one of the most accessible sources of this mineral. A study of more than 5,000 people with early chronic kidney disease associated a high potassium intake with lower blood pressure and slower progression of renal damage. Another reported a 25% lower cardiovascular risk in people consuming more than 3,000 mg of potassium a day.

**Resistant starch: ripeness changes everything.** The green or barely ripe banana contains resistant starch, which escapes digestion in the small intestine and behaves like a prebiotic fibre: it feeds the colonic microbiota and slows the release of glucose into the blood. As the banana ripens, this starch converts into simple sugars — so the same fruit does not have the same metabolic profile depending on the day you eat it.

**Physical exertion.** A study comparing the banana with a 6% carbohydrate drink over a 75 km cycling trial found **no difference** either in blood glucose or in performance. For equal effect, the banana additionally supplies fibre, potassium and antioxidants that a sports drink does not contain.

**A precaution.** An energy-dense, sweet fruit when fully ripe: people with diabetes or watching their weight do well to favour less ripe bananas, with a lower glycaemic index, and to measure the quantity.

## The point to keep

Described in Paradise as a fruit "neither limited nor forbidden", it is today one of the most universally available foods — and a food for exertion whose effectiveness matches, in trial, that of industrial sports drinks.

chapters.title: La jujube
chapters.cat: Les aliments cités dans le Coran
chapters.text:
## In the Qur'an

The lote tree (*sidr*) shares with the banana the verse describing the abode of the "companions of the right":

*"The companions of the right, that blessed company, will dwell among lote trees with thorns removed and banana trees layered with fruit, under extended shade, beside water flowing without cease."* (Qur'an 56:27-33)

The detail matters: *sidr makhdud*, a lote tree **without thorns**. The earthly tree is formidably thorny; in Paradise it is stripped of what wounds. An image of perfection restored.

The lote tree returns in an altogether different register, at the outermost limit of the created world:

*"And he certainly saw him in another descent, at the Lote Tree of the Utmost Boundary, near it is the Garden of Refuge."* (Qur'an 53:13-15)

The *Sidrat al-Muntaha*, the "Lote Tree of the Utmost Boundary", marks the final point reached during the Night Journey — beyond which no creature passes. The Prophet ﷺ described it, saying that its fruits were as large as jars and its leaves like elephants' ears.

## The tree

*Ziziphus jujuba*, of the Rhamnaceae family, native to China and widespread in North Africa, southern Europe and the Middle East. A thorny shrub reaching 6 to 8 metres, remarkably resistant to drought and frost. Its leaves (*sidr*) are traditionally used across the Muslim world for washing the dead and for ruqya, a use going back to prophetic practice.

The fruit, round or oval, turns from yellow to brick red as it ripens; its white flesh is sweet and fragrant, its skin thin and edible. It is eaten fresh, dried like a date, or as jam.

## What the research says

**A remarkable density of polyphenols.** Analyses place the jujube among the fruits richest in phenolic compounds: about 275 to 541 mg per 85 g, where the cherry — often cited as a benchmark — supplies about 114 mg for the same amount. It is also rich in vitamin C, at levels comparable to or above those of citrus depending on the variety.

**Sleep.** This is the best studied use, above all from the seeds (*Ziziphus jujuba var. spinosa*, the wild variety). A randomised clinical trial reported a significant improvement in sleep quality scores on the Pittsburgh index compared with placebo. The compounds involved are thought to be triterpenoids and saponins — jujuboside A, sanjoinine A — for which a sedative effect has been described, with possible action on serotonin.

**Lipid profile.** Work has observed an increase in HDL (the "good" cholesterol) without a rise in LDL, along with a fall in triglycerides and in C-reactive protein, a marker of inflammation.

**An honest reservation.** The Cleveland Clinic notes it plainly: despite encouraging preliminary results, large-scale research on the jujube remains to be done. The existing trials are small, often conducted on concentrated seed extracts rather than on the fruit eaten as it is.

## The point to keep

The tree that marks the utmost limit of the Night Journey bears a modest fruit that is exceptionally rich in polyphenols — and whose traditional use for sleep is beginning to find an echo in clinical trials.

chapters.title: Le miel
chapters.cat: Les aliments cités dans le Coran
chapters.text:
## In the Qur'an

Honey holds a unique place: an entire sura, *An-Nahl* ("The Bees"), carries the name of its producer, and it is the only food the Qur'an explicitly describes as containing a healing.

*"And your Lord inspired the bee: 'Take for yourself among the mountains, houses, and among the trees and in that which they construct. Then eat from all the fruits and follow the ways of your Lord laid down for you.' There emerges from their bellies a drink of varying colours in which there is healing for people. Indeed in that is a sign for a people who give thought."* (Qur'an 16:68-69)

## In the Sunnah

*"Treat yourselves with the two healers: honey and the Qur'an."*

*"Healing is in three things: a mouthful of honey, an incision of cupping (hijama), and cauterisation by fire — but I forbid my community cauterisation."* (Sahih al-Bukhari)

Abdullah ibn Umar, tradition reports, would smear honey on any wound or ailment he suffered.

## What the research says

Honey is probably the food of prophetic medicine best validated by modern research — to the point of entering hospital practice.

**Children's cough: a Cochrane review.** Cochrane reviews are regarded as the highest level of synthesis in evidence-based medicine. The review *Honey for acute cough in children* (updated 2018) gathers six randomised trials covering 899 children. Its conclusions:
- Honey probably reduces cough frequency more than no treatment (mean difference −1.05; moderate-certainty evidence);
- It does slightly better than diphenhydramine (a common cough suppressant);
- It does no better than dextromethorphan, but no worse either.

In other words: a simple, inexpensive food sits at the level of over-the-counter medicines for acute cough in children.

**Wounds and burns.** Medical-grade honey (sterilised, standardised — Manuka honey being the most studied) is used as a hospital dressing. A Cochrane review of burns reported faster healing of superficial and second-degree burns than with conventional treatments such as silver sulfadiazine. On chronic leg ulcers, by contrast, results are mixed and the evidence insufficient to conclude.

**Why it works.** Three documented mechanisms combine: a very high osmotic pressure that dehydrates bacteria, a natural acidity (pH ~3.9), and the gradual release of hydrogen peroxide by an enzyme in honey, glucose oxidase.

**Two important precautions.**
- Honey is **strictly contraindicated before the age of one**, because of the risk of infant botulism — an infant's digestive tract cannot neutralise any spores present.
- Honey is still sugar: about 80% carbohydrate, essentially fructose and glucose. It is not a "neutral" substitute for sugar for someone with diabetes and calls for the same moderation.

## The point to keep

The one food the Qur'an presents as carrying healing is also the one whose usefulness modern research confirms most clearly — for children's cough and for wounds, with evidence of the highest methodological level.

chapters.title: La nigelle (graine noire)
chapters.text:
## In the Sunnah

Black seed (*habba sawda*, the black grain — *Nigella sativa*) is not mentioned in the Qur'an. It holds, however, a place apart in the prophetic tradition, carried by one of the most famous hadiths of the medicine of the Prophet ﷺ:

*"Use this black seed, for it contains a cure for every disease except death."* (Reported by Abu Hurayra — Sahih al-Bukhari, Sahih Muslim)

Transmitted by the two most rigorously authenticated collections in Sunni Islam, this hadith has generated, for a simple kitchen seed, scientific interest without equal: several hundred clinical trials have been published since the 1960s.

## What the research says

This is where prophetic medicine meets the largest volume of human clinical data — and the picture is solid, provided one stays precise.

**A meta-analysis of 82 randomised trials.** A synthesis assessed by the GRADE method (the current standard for judging the quality of evidence), covering 82 randomised controlled trials, concludes that supplementation with *Nigella sativa* significantly improves body mass index, blood pressure and lipid profile, reduces inflammatory markers and improves glycaemic control. The optimal dose identified is about **3 g a day for 12 weeks**.

**Blood pressure.** An earlier meta-analysis of eleven randomised trials (860 participants) reports a mean fall in systolic pressure of about 7.7 mmHg and in diastolic pressure of about 4.9 mmHg after an average of 8 weeks of treatment — that is, relative to control groups, a difference of about −3.3 mmHg (systolic) and −2.8 mmHg (diastolic).

**Blood glucose.** An updated meta-analysis of thirty randomised trials shows a significant reduction in fasting blood glucose and in HbA1c (the marker of glycaemic control over three months). No significant effect, however, was found on insulinaemia or on HOMA-IR, an index of insulin resistance — the precision matters.

**The active compound.** Thymoquinone, the main active principle of black seed oil, concentrates most of the laboratory research for its antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties.

**Where to draw the line.** These results are real and measured, but they concern biological markers — blood pressure, blood glucose, lipids, inflammation — in populations often already at risk. They do not show that black seed cures an established disease, and they replace no prescribed treatment. The hadith uses a register that goes beyond the clinical frame; the studies, for their part, measure what they can measure. The two answer one another without being confused.

**Precautions.** Black seed oil can interact with antihypertensive and antidiabetic treatments, whose effect it may amplify — hence the need to discuss it with a doctor if you are on treatment. Caution is likewise advised during pregnancy.

## How it is taken

Whole seeds chewed or sprinkled on food, an infusion, or cold-pressed oil taken as a course — sometimes mixed with honey, a traditional pairing that brings together the two most cited remedies of the Sunnah.

## The point to keep

Of all the prophetic remedies, black seed has the largest body of human clinical trials — with modest but reproducible effects on blood pressure, blood glucose and inflammation.

chapters.title: L'orge et la talbina
chapters.text:
## In the Sunnah

*"Talbina soothes the heart of the sick and relieves some of their grief."* (Reported by Aisha — Sahih al-Bukhari)

Aisha would have this barley porridge prepared — cooked in milk or water, sweetened with honey — for the sick and the bereaved around her. The word *talbina* comes from *laban*, milk, because of its white, creamy appearance. Ibn Qayyim al-Jawziyya devotes a passage to it in his treatise on prophetic medicine.

Another hadith, also reported by Aisha, specifies the use: when a member of her family died, she would order a pot of talbina to be prepared, then say to the women gathered: *"Eat some of it, for I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: talbina comforts the heart of the sick and dispels some of the grief."*

## What the research says

Barley is one of the few cereals whose health benefit has been formally recognised by health authorities — a level of validation few foods reach.

**A health claim approved on both sides of the Atlantic.** The US *Food and Drug Administration* and the *European Food Safety Authority* (EFSA) both authorise the claim that **3 g a day of beta-glucans** from barley or oats helps reduce blood cholesterol, a risk factor for coronary heart disease. The EFSA opinion (2011) rests on a meta-analysis of twelve randomised controlled trials.

**The size of the effect.** The meta-analyses converge: about 3 g of beta-glucans a day lowers total cholesterol by 0.25 to 0.66 mmol/L and LDL by 0.24 to 0.60 mmol/L, in subjects with normal as well as raised cholesterol. The mechanism is well understood: these soluble fibres form a viscous gel in the gut that traps bile acids, forcing the liver to draw on circulating cholesterol to make new ones.

**Blood glucose and satiety.** EFSA also recognises an effect of barley beta-glucans in reducing postprandial blood glucose — the sugar peak after a meal — by the same mechanism of slowed gastric emptying.

**On mood, let us stay honest.** The hadith speaks of soothing the heart and grief. Barley is rich in fermentable fibre that feeds the gut microbiota, and research on the gut-brain axis is actively exploring the link between microbiota and mood. But no clinical trial has tested talbina itself on anxiety or bereavement: it is a coherent line of thought, not a demonstrated result. The warmth of a comforting dish prepared by loved ones in a time of mourning no doubt produces part of the effect described.

## The point to keep

A dish of mourning and convalescence transmitted by Aisha, whose main ingredient happens to be one of the few dietary fibres to hold a health claim officially validated by both the FDA and EFSA.

chapters.title: Le vinaigre
chapters.text:
## In the Sunnah

Reported by Jabir ibn Abdullah: the Prophet ﷺ asked one day whether there was any condiment in the house. He was told there was only vinegar. He had it brought, ate his bread with it, and said:

*"What an excellent condiment vinegar is! What an excellent condiment vinegar is!"* (Sahih Muslim)

Another hadith reported by Aisha goes the same way: *"What an excellent condiment vinegar is!"* These words carry a particular weight: they honour a modest food, available even in a house without provisions — a lesson in contentment as much as a dietary recommendation.

## What the research says

Vinegar is one of the traditional foods whose metabolic effect is best characterised today.

**Blood glucose after meals.** A meta-analysis of clinical trials published in *Diabetes Research and Clinical Practice* concludes that consuming vinegar significantly reduces postprandial glucose and insulin responses — that is, the sugar and insulin peak that follows a meal.

**The mechanism.** Acetic acid slows gastric emptying: the meal leaves the stomach more gradually, so sugar reaches the blood more slowly. Work published in the *European Journal of Clinical Nutrition* measured this effect directly on a starchy meal. Other research suggests improved insulin sensitivity and glucose uptake by liver and muscle.

**Over time.** In people at increased risk of type 2 diabetes, daily vinegar intake over twelve weeks has been associated with a fall in fasting blood glucose of up to 13%. Long-term results, however, remain inconsistent from one study to another.

**A detail that counts.** A comparative study showed that liquid vinegar (about 25 g) is markedly more effective on blood glucose than the vinegar capsules sold as supplements — the traditional form, on the plate, beats the pharmaceutical one.

**A precaution.** Pure vinegar is acidic: take it diluted or in a dish, never neat by the spoonful, on pain of attacking tooth enamel and the oesophagus.

## The point to keep

A poor man's condiment, praised twice over by the Prophet ﷺ in a house without provisions — and one whose real effect on blood glucose science now measures, provided it is taken as it is, within the meal.

chapters.title: L'eau de Zamzam
chapters.text:
## A water born of a prayer

The Qur'an does not name Zamzam directly, but its origin is present in seed form in Ibrahim's prayer, after he left Hajar and their son Ismail in the barren valley of Makkah:

*"Our Lord, I have settled some of my descendants in an uncultivated valley near Your sacred House…"* (Qur'an 14:37)

Tradition reports that in answer to Hajar's distress, as she ran between the hills of Safa and Marwa to find water for her son, the spring burst forth beneath the child's feet. That course is still retraced today by every pilgrim during the sa'y.

## In the Sunnah

*"The water of Zamzam is for whatever it is drunk for."* (Reported by Jabir ibn Abdullah — Sunan Ibn Majah 3062)

Scholars differ on the degree of authenticity of this hadith: some declare it sound (*sahih*), others weak (*da'if*), the preponderant view upholding its validity. Its import was widely put into practice by the Companions and the generations that followed: Ibn Abbas, on drinking it, would make this supplication — *"O Allah, I ask You for beneficial knowledge, abundant provision and healing from every disease."*

## What scientific analysis says

Zamzam is one of the most analysed waters in the world, its composition having been the subject of several peer-reviewed publications.

**Mineral composition.** A multi-element analysis of 52 elements by inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS), on samples drawn from the fountains of the Sacred Mosque, describes a relatively rich fluoridated mineral water:

| Element | Concentration |
|---|---|
| Sodium | 210 mg/L |
| Calcium | 93 mg/L |
| Sulfate | 64 mg/L |
| Magnesium | 42 mg/L |
| Nitrate | 15.8 mg/L |

**No heavy metals.** The same analysis records extremely low levels of toxic elements: lead (< 0.0005 µg/L), cadmium (< 0.001 µg/L), mercury (< 0.006 µg/L), aluminium (< 0.002 µg/L), arsenic (0.006 µg/L). Published experimental studies report neither hepatic nor renal toxicity.

**Comparison with international standards.** A study published in *Heliyon* (2021) compared seven samples (six from taps, one bottled) with WHO and US EPA reference values. All measured parameters fall below the maximum permissible limits, with one exception: total dissolved solids (TDS), at about 814 mg/L — below the WHO limit (1000 mg/L) but above the EPA's non-binding advisory threshold (500 mg/L). That is characteristic of a frankly mineralised water, not a sign of contamination.

## On the other accounts in circulation

Many claims circulate about Zamzam — about the structure of its water, about properties no analysis measures. This guide deliberately keeps to work published in peer-reviewed journals, the kind whose source the reader can check for themselves. The rest does not appear here: not out of judgement on its content, but because it falls outside that frame.

The merit of Zamzam in Islam is established by the Qur'an, the Sunnah and its sacred status. It stands on its own, needing no outside support.

## The point to keep

A water whose spiritual value rests on the texts, and whose mineral quality is confirmed by published, verifiable analyses.

## The criterion applied

All the references above come from peer-reviewed journals, public medical databases (PubMed, PMC), health agencies (EFSA, FDA), the Cochrane Collaboration, or recognised medical institutions.

Many claims circulate about these foods without ever having been published in that way. This guide's choice is to keep only what the reader can go and check at the source — the rest has therefore been set aside.

## Disclaimer

In case of illness, pregnancy or ongoing treatment, ask your doctor for advice.
